Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan (AE): All right, hi everyone, thanks for joining. I think we have like 45-60 minutes. today we want to focus on the Optimize walkthrough — how adaptive prefetch and batching could change cost for your chat use case. quick intros?
[00:10] Carlos (Customer): Hey, Carlos here. I'm head of ML at Latitude. we run a mixed chat app, a lot of short queries and then long follow-ups. our priority is to keep short request latencies low but we also have heavy nightly batch runs.
[00:20] Maya: Maya — eng manager — mainly concerned about tail latency and SLOs, also about ease of deploying private instances later.
[00:26] Owen: Owen — SRE — I'm the one who will own scaling, curious about how burst works and what telemetry we'll get.
[00:31] Jordan: great. Priya, quick agenda?
[00:34] Priya (SE): Sure. I'll demo the Optimize console scenarios — two simulations: (1) live chat with session affinity + prefix/KV cache, and (2) batch inference with lookahead prefetch turned on. We'll show cost per 1M tokens and latency percentiles, and then Arman will talk about heuristics and rollout policies.
[00:49] Arman (PM): yep, and we'll also cover when Dedicated makes sense vs hosted with burst routing and fallbacks.
[00:55] Jordan: cool. Carlos, before we jump in, quick baseline: what's your current infra? model sizes?
[01:01] Carlos: mostly Llama 3 13B hosted internally on k8s, a mix of quantized and fp16. our peak qps for short queries is about 2k, average about 300, nightly batch jobs can spike to 8k endpoints for a couple hours. right now costs are unpredictable and KV cache isn't implemented.
[01:20] Priya: okay that's helpful. and payload characteristics — average prompt length?
[01:24] Carlos: short queries are 40-80 tokens input, output 20-40 tokens; long threads can be 800-2k tokens.
[01:30] Priya: good — that pattern is one where prefix cache can save a lot on short queries, and lookahead prefetch can reduce repeated prefix compute for multi-turns.
[01:38] Maya: when you say prefix cache, do you mean session KV store or a prefix-only cache? what's the difference in Redwood?
[01:44] Priya: good q — we expose both: prefix cache stores the KV cache for the last n tokens of a request prefix so subsequent requests with the same or similar prefix re-use the KV memory. session KV is per-session and persists KV across turns; there's also a compact 'prefix fingerprint' option that caches only up to X tokens. often customers use a hybrid: prefix caching for common short queries and session KV for deep threads.
[02:03] Owen: is KV stored in-memory on the GPU nodes? any data residency concerns?
[02:08] Arman: KV is managed by the runtime; for Redwood Private/Dedicated we can ensure KV stays within your VPC and add KMS encryption at rest. for hosted, KV eviction policies and retention are configurable.
[02:18] Carlos: ok. show us the console?
[02:21] Priya: jumping into the Optimize console — note the UI labels are approximate in the transcript, I might say Redwood optimal sometimes — (screen share)
[02:30] [screen noise] Priya: top-left is the 'scenario builder' where we upload a traffic histogram. I'm selecting 'Latitude 7d histogram' that you shared earlier. the sim shows simulated cost with baseline (no cache, per-request exec), then scenario A: prefix cache with 1k token window, scenario B: session KV with 30-min TTL, scenario C: adaptive prefetch + batching.
[03:02] Carlos: how accurate are sims vs actual? we had sims from another vendor that were optimistic.
[03:07] Priya: fair. our sims use a runtime-derived token profile and empirical kernel costs from our model catalog; for conservative numbers we give ranges and a 10-15% margin. we also let you upload your own per-token timing CSV to calibrate.
[03:20] Maya: show the numbers for short queries — 95th and 99th latencies?
[03:25] Priya: baseline 95th ~430ms, 99th ~680ms; with prefix cache scenario A 95th ~270ms, 99th ~360ms — and cost per 1M output tokens drops ~34%. with adaptive prefetch + batching we get cost down a further 12% but 95th edges up slightly depending on batch window.
[03:46] Owen: what's adaptive prefetch? is it precomputing ks for likely next-turns?
[03:50] Priya: exactly — the runtime watches session patterns and prefetches KV for predicted next-token windows. heuristics can be conservative or aggressive; conservative means prefetch only when session prob > 0.7 and only small windows. aggressive can prefetch larger contexts but may increase compute and memory cost.
[04:07] Carlos: interesting. what about cold-starts — will prefetching make them worse?
[04:11] Priya: cold-starts can see a small extra cost if prefetch triggers unnecessarily; that's why the console provides expected false-positive rate and a break-even analysis. typically prefix caching gives immediate wins for short queries with high reuse.
[04:24] Jordan: can we talk about batching and latency budget? Carlos said 99th must be under 350ms for short queries — prefix helped but 99th in your numbers was 360ms. what levers do we have?
[04:36] Priya: a couple: (1) reduce batch window (less batching improves tail latency but costs more), (2) use per-route latency SLAs to route latency-sensitive traffic to a low-latency pool (smaller batch sizes, higher cost), (3) hybrid: route 95% of short queries through prefix cache+default pool and 5% through dedicated low-latency pool for tail-critical flows.
[04:56] Maya: the hybrid routing sounds complex — what's the ops overhead?
[05:00] Arman: it's policy driven in the control plane — you set a routing rule by tag (e.g., api-route=short-critical) and the router will prefer low-latency pool. failover policies are automatic. ops burden is minimal: it's configuration, not code change.
[05:12] Owen: are these pools hosted or can they be Dedicated? we may prefer Dedicated for PII workloads.
[05:17] Jordan: both. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity — lower jitter and predictable throughput. Hosted with routing and fallbacks is cheaper initially but can have more variability in latency in extreme bursts.
[05:29] Carlos: ok let's run a hypothetical: assume 2k peak qps short queries, 300 avg, want 99th <350ms, and cost target is sub-$1.50 per 1k responses — is that feasible?
[05:42] Priya: running quick sim: baseline no-cache cost per 1k responses about $2.30. with prefix cache tuned to high reuse and a small dedicated tail pool for 7% of traffic, we get to $1.28 per 1k responses and 99th ~330ms in the sim. numbers depend on model quantization and batching.
[06:02] Carlos: that's promising. what's the impact of model quantization? we currently run q4_0 / int8 on some nodes.
[06:08] Priya: quantization reduces per-token kernel time and memory; recommended on Dedicated for cost-sensitive paths. Optimize suggests quantization profile per model based on your quality evals. we surfaced a 2% quality delta on long threads for q4 vs fp16 in your model family — you'd need to test.
[06:24] Maya: do you provide an A/B rollout for quality regressions?
[06:27] Arman: yes — our rollout features let you split traffic by percent, compare logits-level diffs and run evaluation sets. Console also ties quality regressions to alerts.
[06:35] Owen: security Qs — SAML SSO, audit logs, and KMS integration — can you summarize?
[06:40] Jordan: for Dedicated/Private we support SAML SSO, fine-grained RBAC, audit logs shipped to your logging endpoint, and KMS/HSM integrations for key management. we'll follow up with SOC2/ISO artifacts.
[06:51] Carlos: good. any caveats for lookahead prefetch and GDPR/PPI concerns?
[06:56] Arman: prefetch operates on prediction of next tokens and does not externalize user data. for Private deployments, KV stays inside your VPC; we recommend TTLs and redaction rules for sensitive fields.
[07:08] Jen (Product): I also want to understand developer workflow — how do engineers instrument policies? is there SDK?
[07:12] Priya: SDKs include annotations on requests (session_id, route tag). the Optimize console will ingest traffic and produce recommended policies (batch window, prefetch aggressiveness, prefix token window) as JSON you can apply via API.
[07:23] Carlos: show me a policy example?
[07:25] Priya: sure — (reads aloud) route: short-critical, prefetch: conservative, prefix_window: 128, session_ttl: 30m, batch_max_wait_ms: 12, fallback: dedicated-pool-1. the actual JSON is downloadable.
[07:40] [laptop clack]
[07:43] Maya: what about ops metrics — what will SRE see on dashboards?
[07:46] Priya: per-route token cost, batch sizes distribution, cache hit rates, prefetch false-positive rate, latency p50/p95/p99, and per-model kernel time. there are also traces linking token cost to specific requests.
[07:59] Owen: can we export those to Prometheus?
[08:01] Priya: yes, metrics export and alerting hooks available for Dedicated and Private; hosted has a push endpoint and retained metrics in Console.
[08:09] Jordan: let's pivot to deployment plan — what would a 6-week pilot look like?
[08:13] Priya: week 0-1: onboarding + traffic histogram + sandbox sim; week 2: run baseline A/B on a small fraction of traffic using hosted with prefix cache; week 3-4: expand to more traffic and enable adaptive prefetch (conservative); week 5: analyze quality/regression; week 6: decision to move to Dedicated or full rollout.
[08:31] Carlos: that matches what we need. any prerequisites?
[08:34] Priya: sample traffic, schema for session ids, and a short eval set for quality checks. access for Redwood to a limited telemetry export (S3 or signed URL) to calibrate sims.
[08:45] Carlos: we'll try to get that this week.
[08:48] Jordan: objections? cost risks?
[08:50] Maya: only concern is prefetch giving us surprises in spikes.
[08:53] Priya: we mitigate via throttles, TTLs and conservative heuristics. the console shows expected extra compute if prefetch rate is X.
[08:59] [pause]
[09:05] Priya: quick demo deeper dive — I'm switching to the cost-sim tab. here's a stacked bar for compute, memory, and infra. note the 'prefetch overhead' slice appears only in adaptive scenario. you can slide prefetch sensitivity from 0-100 and watch cost/latency curves.
[09:26] Carlos: can you export a CSV?
[09:28] Priya: yes — export CSV and a shareable sandbox link that your team can run. I'll include that in the follow-up.
[09:35] Arman: also calling out the 'break glass' policy: if tail latency crosses threshold, requests automatically reroute to low-latency pool. that's an auto-failover.
[09:45] Owen: good. what about burst capacity for nightly batch runs? we'd like to avoid pre-provisioning for occasional spikes.
[09:51] Jordan: two options: (1) reserved Dedicated capacity sized for steady-state and rely on hosted burst for extreme spikes, or (2) Reserved + autoscaling burst with scheduled capacity reservations for known windows. pricing differs.
[10:03] Carlos: which is cheaper overall?
[10:05] Priya: if spikes are infrequent and predictable, reserved for steady-state + hosted burst is usually cheapest. if you need strict SLA during spikes, then Dedicated reservations sized for spikes are better. we'll show both in the TCO note.
[10:17] Maya: show an example TCO?
[10:19] Priya: (switches tab) example: baseline annual for hosted-only $X, Reserved Dedicated for peak windows adds $Y but reduces per-token by ~30% in sustained usage. I'll attach a spreadsheet.
[10:33] Carlos: any gotchas with session affinity and horizontal scaling?
[10:36] Priya: session affinity pins a session to a pool/node to keep KV hot; that can reduce reuse across nodes but improves latency. we balance via session TTL and rebalancing windows.
[10:47] Jen: what's the expected engineering lift? 2 engineers for a month?
[10:51] Jordan: for a pilot we estimate 1 engineer ~3-4 weeks to instrument SDK and run sim, SRE time for telemetry is smaller. full rollout depends on model migration.
[10:59] Carlos: okay. any limitations with our model family (Llama3 13B) and quantized inference?
[11:03] Priya: we have verified kernels for q4, q8 where applicable, and Optimize will pick kernels accordingly. for some edge ops there can be slightly higher latency with q8, but cost wins often outweigh. we'll surface model-variant compatibility.
[11:16] Maya: competitor question — we trialed Vendor X and their caching felt manual. how is Redwood different?
[11:21] Arman: main difference is runtime-integrated caching + automatic policy suggestions from Optimize plus first-class rollout and tracing. console automation reduces manual tuning.
[11:31] Carlos: thanks. let's do a quick recap and action items.
[11:34] Jordan: recap: Redwood to share sandbox sim CSV, pricing note, Dedicated tier examples. Latitude to share 7-day histogram & sample payloads and security questions. follow up pilot kickoff week of 6/22.
[11:47] Priya: I'll attach the scenario export and a quick how-to for running an adaptive-prefetch sim in your sandbox.
[11:52] Owen: I'll draft security questions and confirm logs access.
[11:55] Carlos: great. Jordan, any closing notes?
[11:58] Jordan: just we'll aim to get the sim to you by EOD Tuesday, I'll include pricing, and Priya will run the live sim. thanks everyone.
